title: Trades With a Rest Day
statement:
You get prices, where prices[i] is the price of one share on day i. You may trade as often as you like, under three rules:

  • You hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before you buy again.
  • Each day you do at most one thing: buy, sell, or nothing.
  • After a day on which you sell, you must rest the next day: no buying on the day right after a sale.

Return the largest total profit you can make. Doing nothing at all is allowed and earns 0.

examples.why: Buying at 1 and selling at 6 earns 5. Selling at 5 forces a rest on the day priced 1; trading 2→5 and then 4→6 also earns only 5. Taking every rise, as without the rule, would claim 8.
Prices only fall, so the best plan is never to trade.
Sell early at 3, rest on the 5, buy at 2 and sell at 9: 2 + 7. Grabbing the bigger first trade 1→5 or 1→8 leaves at most 7.

hints: On any day you are in one of a few situations: holding a share, just sold today, or free with no share. Which situations can lead to which the next day?
Let dp[i][s] be the best profit after day i if you end that day in state s: hold, sold (sold today) or rest (no share, did not sell today). Write each from the states of day i−1.

hold = max(hold, rest − p), sold = hold + p, rest = max(rest, sold), all from yesterday's values. You can only buy from rest, never straight from sold: that is the rest-day rule. The answer is max(sold, rest) on the last day.

explain.intuition:
The table here has one axis for time and one for the situation you are in. Let dp[i][s] be the best profit after day i, ending the day in state s. Three states are enough: hold (you own a share), sold (you sold today, so tomorrow you must rest) and rest (no share, and you did not sell today, so you are free to buy tomorrow).

Read each entry off the last decision, the one taken on day i. You hold today if you already held yesterday and did nothing, or you were in rest yesterday and bought today: max(hold[i−1], rest[i−1] − p[i]). You are sold today only if you held yesterday and sold: hold[i−1] + p[i]. You are in rest today if yesterday was rest or sold and you did nothing: max(rest[i−1], sold[i−1]). Notice that there is no arrow from sold to hold; that missing arrow is the rest-day rule. It is a small state machine, like a UI component that can be idle, loading or cooling down, with the table storing the best score for each state at each step.
steps: For each later day with price p, compute the new values from the old ones at the same time.
hold' = max(hold, rest − p), sold' = hold + p, rest' = max(rest, sold).
Replace the old values with the new ones.
Return max(sold, rest). Ending in hold is never better: that share was paid for and never sold.
pitfalls: Updating hold from today's sold or rest after already overwriting them. All three must read yesterday's values; save them first.
Letting hold come from sold. That drops the rest day and gives 8 instead of 5 on the first example.
Being greedy about the first trade. In the third example the larger first trade blocks a much better second one.

solutions.title: Try every choice, day by day
solutions.idea: f(i, holding): either do nothing today, or buy (if free) / sell (if holding, then skip tomorrow). No memory, so the number of calls grows exponentially.

solutions.title: Table of days × states
solutions.idea: dp[i] = [hold, sold, rest] after day i, each read off the decision taken on day i.

solutions.title: Three running values
solutions.idea: Day i reads only day i − 1, so keep three numbers and update them together.

followups: Instead of a rest day, every sale costs a fixed fee. Which arrow of the state machine changes?
The rest period is k days instead of one. How many states do you need now, or can you look further back in the table instead?
Return the actual days to buy and sell, not just the profit.
